Arnold Schoenberg, born in 1874 and died in 1951, was an Austrian-born composer, music theorist, and painter who was one of the most radical and influential figures of twentieth-century music. He led the Second Viennese School and pioneered the abandonment of traditional key signatures through atonality. To organize this new harmonic space, Schoenberg invented the twelve-tone technique, also called dodecaphony, a system of composition using serial rows of all twelve chromatic pitches. His works moved from lush late-Romanticism to dramatic Expressionism and full serialism, generating intense public controversy and permanently altering the course of music history.

The twelve-tone technique is a compositional system in which a piece is built upon a specific permutation of the twelve notes of the chromatic scale, manipulated through inversion, retrograde, and retrograde-inversion. The Second Viennese School refers to Schoenberg and his two most famous pupils, Alban Berg, composer of the opera Wozzeck, and Anton Webern, known for his sparse, brief pointillist works. Schoenberg coined the term emancipation of the dissonance to describe his harmonic philosophy, arguing that dissonance no longer needed to resolve to consonance, treating all intervals as equally stable.

Among his major compositions, Pierrot Lunaire from 1912 is an Expressionist setting of twenty-one poems for female reciter and a chamber ensemble, famous for utilizing Sprechstimme, a vocal style where the performer strictly follows the rhythm but slides between pitches, halfway between speaking and singing. Verklärte Nacht, or Transfigured Night from 1904, is an early, lush late-Romantic string sextet based on a poem by Richard Dehmel, depicting a couple walking in a forest. Gurrelieder is a massive, late-Romantic cantata requiring colossal orchestral and choral forces, over four hundred performers, representing his transition to his mature style. Moses und Aron is his major, unfinished twelve-tone opera, depicting the biblical conflict between Moses, who only speaks, and Aaron, who sings lyrically. A Survivor from Warsaw, written in 1947, is a dramatic cantata for narrator, male chorus, and orchestra, depicting the Holocaust in the Warsaw Ghetto, concluding with the singing of the Shema Yisrael.

Born into a Jewish family in Vienna, Schoenberg converted to Lutheranism in his youth but formally returned to Judaism in Paris in 1933 after fleeing Nazi Germany. He emigrated to the United States, settling in Los Angeles and teaching at USC and UCLA. He suffered from severe triskaidekaphobia, the fear of the number thirteen, ironically dying on Friday, July thirteenth, 1951, at thirteen minutes before midnight. He pioneered serialism and atonality in the twentieth century, and his early works like Verklärte Nacht were strongly influenced by Johannes Brahms and Richard Wagner. In exile, he re-embraced his Jewish heritage in response to the rise of Nazism, composing several explicitly Jewish works.
